subject: Zero-trust handoff patterns: Transit hub vs PrivateLink vs IPSec
messages:
From: Vanessa Ortiz <vanessa_ortiz@redwood.com>
To: Sanjay Patel <sanjay@acmecorp.com>; ACME NetSec Team <netsec@acmecorp.com>
Cc: Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwood.com>, Kimberly Park <kimberly_park@redwood.com>, Karthik Iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.com>
Date: Tue, 25 May 2027 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: Zero-trust handoff patterns: Transit hub vs PrivateLink vs IPSec

Hi Sanjay / ACME NetSec,

Thanks again for the time this morning. Per our discussion, I wanted to put a short, pragmatic note on three handoff patterns for Redwood Private (VPC/on-prem) deployments and call out the operational tradeoffs we see most often:

1) Transit / hub VPC (peering or Transit Gateway)
   - Pros: Low-latency, simple for multi-region multi-VPC topologies, supports full bidirectional flows if you need service discovery.
   - Cons: Surface area is larger (routing table sprawl), requires careful CIDR planning and route propagation controls for least privilege.

2) AWS PrivateLink / Interface Endpoints
   - Pros: Narrower attack surface (only endpoint ENIs), easier to enforce per-service IAM and security groups, clear egress paths for auditing.
   - Cons: Slightly higher per-connection latency vs direct peering for chatty token-cookie workloads; requires endpoint service configuration and private DNS considerations.

3) IPSec site-to-site VPN (customer gateway + VGW or equivalent)
   - Pros: Works for on-prem and cloud alike, quick pilot without cloud account changes, easy to co-manage with existing customers that already have VPNs.
   - Cons: Less predictable latency and throughput, harder to scale to high concurrency without HA tunnels or SD-WAN.

Operational considerations we should align on for ACME:
- Zero-trust: do you want an ingress model where only specific endpoints can reach the Redwood control/data plane? PrivateLink gives the tightest per-service boundaries; transit requires additional firewall appliances or SG rules.
- Observable handoff: we can emit token-level audit logs and source IPs; some customers prefer PrivateLink because it reduces shared VPC telemetry noise.
- Backplane for stateful flows: if you plan to host routing/coordination with internal services that call back into models often, peering/transit tends to have better performance.

I've attached a checklist and a quick comparison matrix to help the team pick. Can the NetSec team confirm which constraints are hard blockers (e.g., no cross-VPC routing, must restrict to LB IPs only, MTU limits)? We can then produce a config-first sample for your team.

Next steps I propose:
- Sanjay / Rajeev: confirm the two must-have security controls.
- ACME NetSec: share any existing SAML/KMS constraints we should be aware of.
- Redwood (Ben/Kim): we will draft a minimal PrivateLink blueprint and an alternative hub VPC blueprint with route-lockdown examples.

Thanks,

Vanessa Ortiz
Customer Solutions
Redwood Inference

Subject: Re: Zero-trust handoff patterns: Transit hub vs PrivateLink vs IPSec

Vanessa —

Thanks for the clear summary. A couple of questions from our side before we lock a pattern:

- Our compliance group will push back on any design that requires broad VPC routing across business units. They prefer minimal surface area per app. So PrivateLink sounds appealing.
- We need to understand MTU and fragmentation implications — our appliances enforce 1400 MTU today on the MPLS circuits.
- For PrivateLink, how do you handle DNS discovery for model endpoints? We have internal name resolution rules and don't want to break existing split-horizon DNS.

If you can answer these three items and share a sample CloudFormation/Terraform fragment for an endpoint service, that will help us decide.

Sanjay
NetSec Lead, AcmeCorp

Sanjay —

Quick answers from an implementation/ops lens:

- Surface area: agree with your compliance preference. PrivateLink is the lowest blast radius and maps well to a zero-trust posture. You can scope endpoints per account/team and enforce SGs and endpoint policies.
- MTU: PrivateLink doesn't change path MTU itself; the ENI traffic flows over the VPC network. If you have 1400 enforced on the on-prem side, you'll want to set PMTU discovery and avoid jumbo frames on the appliance. We'll include sample iptables/iptables-mangle and ipsec configs.
- DNS: two common patterns:
   a) Private DNS override — the endpoint service injects a private hosted zone and you configure split-horizon to resolve the service name to the endpoint ENI IPs.
   b) Client-side hosts — small teams sometimes map the specific endpoint IPs in DNS entries for strict control. We prefer (a) because it scales.

I'll put together a minimal Terraform module for a regional PrivateLink endpoint and a Transit-GW peering example with route filters so you can see the differences side-by-side.

—Ben
Sr. Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference

Thanks all — couple clarifying points from NetOps:

- MTU: Confirmed — our edge enforces 1400. Any long-lived TLS connections should be resilient but we'll run perf tests.
- Logging: we need to see connection-level logs with source principal (OIDC/SAML) and source IP. Will PrivateLink preserve client IPs for audit purposes, or do you require a proxy layer?
- Failover: if we go with PrivateLink, what is the recommended HA layout for cross-AZ outage scenarios?

If you can include logging behavior and an HA diagram in the sample config, that would be ideal.

Regards,
Rajeev

Appreciate the details — we've captured the asks and attached a short packet that covers:
- PrivateLink blueprint (Terraform fragment + DNS pattern + HA recommendations)
- Transit/Hub blueprint with route-lockdown examples and firewall placement notes
- IPsec VPN checklist with MTU and throughput mitigation tips
- Logging & audit patterns that show where source principal and IP can be captured (Redwood emits request-level metadata to the customer-controlled logging sink; when operating through PrivateLink you keep source IPs via ENI preservation but if you terminate at a proxy you'll see proxied IPs — the packet explains both).

3) If VPN: we'll send a pre-built ipsec config and a run-of-the-mill throughput validation plan.
